results.result: The study examined a cohort of 38 patients after autoimmune limbic encephalitis, with 34/38 meeting criteria for 'definite LE', 28/38 having identified autoantibodies, and 31/38 having received immunotherapy in the acute phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C33, C90-C95 provide consistent descriptive data about the patient cohort. The sample characteristics are clearly documented with specific numbers and diagnostic criteria, representing standard methodological reporting for a clinical study.

results.result: Acute clinical MRI findings showed that 34/38 patients had abnormal hippocampal signal/volume, with inflammatory changes appearing confined to the hippocampus in the vast majority of patients, and no acute inflammatory changes in the thalamus.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 and C96-C107 are well-supported by clinical MRI data from the acute phase and citations to prior literature. The focal nature of acute hippocampal pathology is documented both in this cohort and in referenced studies, providing converging evidence.

results.result: Patients showed highly focal episodic memory impairment with deficits in recall and recognition of verbal and visual material, pronounced visual forgetting, impaired remote autobiographical memory, but preserved face recognition, semantic memory, language, visuomotor and executive function.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C51 are supported by comprehensive neuropsychological assessment data presented in Table 1, with appropriate statistical comparisons between patients and controls. The pattern of selective episodic memory impairment with preserved other cognitive functions is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Volumetric analysis revealed pronounced bilateral hippocampal atrophy (left: F=46.02, p<0.0005; right: F=63.38, p<0.0005), right entorhinal cortical volume reduction (F=10.76, p=0.0308), and left thalamic volume reduction (F=15.41, p=0.0003), confirmed by whole-brain VBM showing reduced gray matter in hippocampus and thalamic regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are well-supported by both manual volumetry (Table 3) and VBM analysis (Table 4, Figure 2a), with significant statistical results and convergent findings across methods. The structural abnormalities are clearly documented with appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons.

results.result: Patients showed reduced resting-state amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (rsALFF) in the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, with the effect of hippocampal volume reduction on PCC rsALFF fully mediated by thalamic volume reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by resting-state fMRI analysis (Figure 2b-c) and mediation analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The mediation finding is particularly important as it demonstrates the network cascade from hippocampus to thalamus to PCC, consistent with known anatomical connectivity.

results.result: Connectome-MVPA analysis identified a right hippocampal cluster showing abnormal whole-brain functional connectivity, with reduced rsFC to medial prefrontal cortex, posteromedial cortex, and left hippocampus. Inter-hippocampal rsFC negatively correlated with delay since symptom onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are supported by data-driven connectome-MVPA analysis (Figure 2d) followed by seed-to-voxel analysis (Figure 2e-g). The temporal correlation with symptom onset (C66) provides additional support for the hypothesis that network abnormalities develop following hippocampal damage.

results.result: Verbal recognition scores correlated with reduced inter-hippocampal rsFC (r=0.498, p-corr=0.039), and inter-hippocampal rsFC was the only predictor of verbal recognition in stepwise regression (R²=0.25, p=0.003), explaining variance beyond hippocampal volume.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 3b) and multiple stepwise regression. The finding that inter-hippocampal connectivity predicts verbal recognition beyond hippocampal volume is statistically robust and addresses the study's hypothesis about network contributions to memory.

results.result: Visual recognition scores correlated with reduced PCC rsALFF (r=0.543, p-corr=0.014), and the effects of left hippocampal volume reduction on visual recognition were fully mediated by PCC rsALFF reduction (indirect effect: β=0.21, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.41).
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are supported by correlation analysis and mediation analysis (Figure 4). The mediation finding demonstrates that PCC functional abnormalities explain the relationship between hippocampal atrophy and visual recognition, supporting the network hypothesis.

results.result: Verbal recall correlated with both PCC rsALFF (r=0.582, p-corr=0.004) and left hippocampal volume (r=0.495, p-corr=0.024), with the effects of hippocampal atrophy fully mediated by PCC rsALFF reduction (indirect effect: β=0.14, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.29).
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by correlation and mediation analyses (Figure 5). The full mediation by PCC rsALFF is consistent with findings for visual recognition and verbal recall, demonstrating a common network mechanism for recall memory deficits.

results.result: The effects of hippocampal atrophy on visual recall were fully mediated by PCC rsALFF reduction (indirect effect: β=0.19, 95% CI: 0.01, 0.46).
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by mediation analysis (Figure 6). The finding extends the pattern of PCC-mediated effects to visual recall, though the confidence interval is wider and the effect marginally significant, suggesting this may be a weaker relationship than for verbal recall.

results.result: Visual forgetting scores correlated only with right hippocampal volume (VBM: rho=0.556, p-corr=0.008; manual: rho=0.508, p-corr=0.026), and this effect remained direct and unmediated by PCC rsALFF (direct effect: β=0.43, p=0.036; indirect effect: β=0.10, 95% CI: -0.11, 0.32).
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C79-C80 are supported by correlation and mediation analyses (Figure 7). This is a critical finding showing that forgetting, unlike recall and recognition, has a direct relationship with hippocampal volume that is not mediated by network abnormalities, distinguishing it from other memory processes.

results.result: Remote autobiographical memory scores correlated with left thalamic volume (r=0.558, p-corr=0.041), and the effects of left hippocampal atrophy were fully mediated by thalamic volume reduction (indirect effect: β=0.82, 95% CI: 0.20, 1.89).
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C81 are supported by correlation and mediation analyses (Figure 8). The full mediation by thalamic volume suggests that remote memory deficits are explained by thalamic pathology rather than direct hippocampal effects, which has important theoretical implications for consolidation theories.

results.result: Associations of hippocampal volume with recall, recognition, and remote memory were fully mediated by wider network abnormalities, with only forgetting showing a direct relationship with hippocampal atrophy. The forgetting of newly learned information was the most sensitive and specific measure to hippocampal atrophy.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 and C145-C147 represent the study's main conclusions, which are well-supported by the pattern of mediation analyses across multiple memory domains. The distinction between mediated (recall, recognition, remote memory) and direct (forgetting) effects is consistently demonstrated across analyses.

results.result: The study predicted that hippocampal damage would be accompanied by remote network abnormalities, that these would explain memory variability beyond hippocampal atrophy, that relationships would be mediated by network disruption, and that this would enable identification of direct hippocampal effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 state the study's a priori hypotheses, which are clearly articulated and subsequently tested. The predictions are well-grounded in prior literature on extended hippocampal networks and are systematically addressed by the study's analyses.

results.result: Extra-hippocampal structures within the extended hippocampal system (thalamus, PCC) are affected as a secondary consequence of hippocampal damage, with the temporal correlation between inter-hippocampal rsFC and delay since symptom onset supporting this interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108 and C116 represent interpretations of the cross-sectional data. While the acute MRI findings (C105-C106) show focal hippocampal pathology and the temporal correlation (C66) is suggestive, the cross-sectional design cannot definitively establish causality. Longitudinal studies are needed to confirm this interpretation.

results.result: The hippocampal role in amnesia may be less direct than previously held for standardized memory tests, with hippocampal circuitry acting as a buffer for temporary maintenance while non-hippocampal structures store permanent traces. Understanding network-wide changes is key to resolving controversies in amnesia research.
results.evaluation: Claims C130, C132, C138-C139, and C148 represent the study's theoretical conclusions. These are well-supported by the pattern of findings showing mediated effects for most memory processes and direct effects only for forgetting, though alternative interpretations (e.g., regarding mind-wandering) are acknowledged.

results.result: Hippocampal amnesia has played a fundamental role in memory neuroscience since patient H.M., but studies have produced inconsistent results and been criticized for not considering that focal hippocampal damage may trigger network-wide abnormalities, which are documented in stroke and small amnesia case series but remain under-explored.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the rationale for the study by documenting the historical importance of hippocampal amnesia research, the inconsistencies in the literature, and the potential role of network abnormalities.

results.result: The literature contains ongoing debates about whether recall and recognition dissociate (recollection vs. familiarity), whether hippocampal processing is material-specific, whether abnormal forgetting occurs after MTL damage, and whether the hippocampus is necessary for remote memory (standard consolidation vs. multiple trace theory).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C17 accurately summarize major theoretical debates in the amnesia literature, supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the theoretical context and controversies that the study aims to address.

results.result: Hippocampal amnesia is very rare, leading most studies to rely on small numbers of cases susceptible to confounds such as impairment severity, measurement noise, and individual differences. Larger cohort studies would partially overcome these confounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 establish the methodological rationale for the study's large cohort approach. The limitations of small-sample studies are well-documented in the cited literature, and the logical inference about benefits of larger samples (C21) is sound.

results.result: Autoimmune limbic encephalitis typically causes focal hippocampal damage that responds to immunotherapy, though some patients develop hippocampal atrophy and persistent anterograde amnesia. Post-mortem and animal studies confirm focal limbic involvement, contrasting with wider damage in other encephalitides or ischemia/anoxia.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 establish autoimmune LE as an appropriate model for studying hippocampal amnesia, supported by extensive citations to clinical, post-mortem, and animal studies. The contrast with other etiologies strengthens the rationale for using this patient population.

results.result: The study used manual volumetry of MTL regions, whole-brain VBM of structural MRI, and resting-state fMRI to identify structural and functional abnormalities. Memory was assessed using composite scores for anterograde retrieval, remote autobiographical memory, and forgetting (Doors and People test).
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 and C101-C104 describe the study's methods, which are clearly documented and appropriate for the research questions. The use of composite scores is justified for data reduction and generalizability, and the Doors and People test's unique approach to measuring forgetting is explained.

results.result: Anterograde retrieval scores correlated with reduced PCC rsALFF (r=0.551, p-corr=0.024).
results.evaluation: Claim C67 reports a significant correlation that survived correction for multiple testing. However, this composite score was later decomposed into more specific memory components (verbal/visual recall/recognition), making this result less informative than the subsequent fine-grained analyses.

results.result: The study's findings are consistent with prior literature showing that face recognition may be processed differently, that posteromedial cortex has a causal role in episodic memory, that inter-hippocampal connectivity relates to memory, and that resting-state fMRI provides reliable correlates of memory impairment. Alternative interpretations regarding mind-wandering are acknowledged.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C125 contextualize the study's findings within existing literature, with appropriate citations. The acknowledgment of alternative interpretations (C124) regarding mind-wandering demonstrates appropriate scientific caution about the mechanisms underlying resting-state findings.

results.result: Rapid forgetting of visual information in right hippocampal damage was noted early in the literature, with recent functional neuroimaging attributing a central role to the hippocampus in constraining forgetting through pattern completion and pattern separation mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 provide theoretical context for the forgetting findings, supported by appropriate citations to both early clinical observations and recent computational models. This contextualizes the study's finding of a direct hippocampal effect on forgetting.

results.result: Tests of accelerated forgetting may have utility in early detection of Alzheimer's disease. Research in autoimmune LE has focused on anterograde memory with little evidence on retrograde amnesia, though the AMI and Autobiographical Interview offer comparable results in other amnesic cohorts.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C137 provide context for the study's findings on forgetting and remote memory, supported by appropriate citations. These claims acknowledge both the potential clinical utility of forgetting measures and limitations of the AMI for assessing episodic aspects of remote memory.

results.result: Focal thalamic damage has been associated with retrograde amnesia, with mediodorsal thalamic nuclei potentially coordinating recollection via thalamic-prefrontal projections. The study's thalamic findings are consistent with developmental amnesia literature, and direct forniceal projections from hippocampus to anterior thalamus exist in primates.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C144 provide anatomical and clinical context for the thalamic findings, supported by appropriate citations. These claims help interpret the mediation of remote memory effects by thalamic volume and suggest directions for future research regarding mammillary body involvement.

results.result: Patients showed impaired recall, recognition, maintenance of new information, and remote autobiographical amnesia, along with reduced thalamic and entorhinal volume, inter-hippocampal connectivity, and posteromedial cortex activity. results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 provide summary statements of the study's main findings. These are well-supported by the detailed analyses presented throughout the results section and represent appropriate high-level conclusions from the data.

results.result: Extra-hippocampal damage is equally or more likely in other conditions associated with hippocampal amnesia (ischemia/anoxia), though one post-mortem case showed focal CA1 neuronal loss. Patients showed functional abnormalities in posteromedial cortex consistent with prior observations in hippocampal and diencephalic amnesias.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 acknowledge limitations and provide context for interpreting the study's findings. The acknowledgment of the Zola-Morgan case (C110) showing focal pathology demonstrates appropriate scientific caution, while C111-C112 connect findings to prior literature.

results.result: In healthy individuals, the hippocampus shows coupled spontaneous activity with the contralateral hippocampus and forms part of the default-mode network, as do the medial prefrontal and posteromedial cortical regions that showed reduced connectivity with the hippocampus in patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 provide established neuroscientific context for interpreting the functional connectivity findings, supported by appropriate citations to foundational default-mode network literature. This contextualizes the observed reductions in connectivity.
